lines.text: A landlocked country of the West African savanna, of Mossi kings, a revolutionary captain and a troubled present. This is the story of Burkina Faso.
About a thousand years ago, people raised the stone walls of Loropeni, a settlement tied to the gold trade, now a World Heritage Site.
From around the twelfth century, the Mossi kingdoms took hold of the plateau, and held out for centuries against Mali and Songhai.
Ouagadougou became the seat of their emperor, the Mogho Naba, and is the capital still.
France conquered the Mossi in 1896, and in 1919 made the land a colony called Upper Volta.
In 1921 Maurice Yameogo was born, who would become the country's first president.
In 1949 Thomas Sankara was born, the young captain who would take power and give his country a new name.
Two years later came Blaise Compaore, his comrade, and later the man who would seize power from him.
In 1960 Upper Volta won its independence from France.
In 1965, in the village of Gando, Francis Kere was born, the architect who would win the Pritzker Prize.
In 1969 Ouagadougou began to host FESPACO, the great festival of African cinema.
In 1988, a year after Sankara was killed, Ibrahim Traore was born. He would take power in a coup in 2022.
In 2014, after twenty-seven years, a popular uprising drove Compaore from power.
And in 2023, amid jihadist attacks and military rule, Burkina Faso joined Mali and Niger in a new alliance, turning away from France.
The land of upright people still searches for peace and its own way forward.
